speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
maintopic: STRIKE OF BARTENDERS IN ALBERTA
speechtext:
On May 8 I made a statement to the house on the coal situation and pointed out that unless the production of bituminous coal was resumed in the United States in the near future the Canadian position would be most serious.
Since that time, the miners have agreed to-resume work for a truce period of two weeks, a period which expires to-morrow. In spite of the truce, many of the mines, and particularly those in Pennsylvania which supply large tonnages to Canada, did not resume production. The United States government took over the mines on Thursday, but no information is available as to what effect this action will have on the future production of coal.
lesterday, as the house is aware, strike-action by a section of the United States railway employees paralysed the whole rail transportation system of the United States. This action will result in a complete stoppage of coal production in the United States mines, and will also prevent the delivery of any coal that is at present en route to Canada. The implications of this action are so far-reaching that it is impossible-to make any forecast of the effect upon our coal position, except to
Coal-Supply Situation

say that it makes a bad situation very much worse. The whole problem is at present being most carefully reviewed, and I shall advise the house later of the action considered neces-sarj' to give the greatest possible protection to our industry and people.
I believe the house should be informed of the situation facing this country before the railway strike occurred. The truce in the coal fields, unfortunately, caused soma Canadian consumers to believe that our troubles were over, but the facts of the case did not give any basis for such optimism.
Last year Canada imported some 2.979,000 tons of United States bituminous coal in the seven weeks from April 1 to May 19. In the same seven weeks this year our imports have been 710.000 tons, a straight loss of 2.200.000.. or ten per cent of our estimated needs. That. Mr. Speaker, was the position as at May 19, but it was by no means the whole story. By the end of June, when, if work had continued in the United States mines, coal should have become freely available, our deficiency as against last year would have risen to almost five and one-half million tons, or one-quarter of our estimated requirements of bituminous coal in the central provinces. The point I would, emphasize is that we were facing this *deficiency -under the best of circumstances, *that is, the maintenance of full production.
During the summer months the vessels in 'the -great lakes are usually employed to capa-*city in carrying coal, and the loss of some .three months of navigation forms a handicap that, can never be fully recovered. It was planned to use the rail facilities to the utmost, but even here there was a very definite limit and it did appear that at the end of the twelvemonth period, at March 31 next year, we would only have received from eighteen to nineteen million tons to supply a requirement of approximately twenty-two million tons.
That, Mr. Speaker, was the basis for present orders restricting the consumption of coal. There are many consumers throughout the country who are well aware of the danger, and see clearly that five weeks' production of coal cannot be lost without serious effect. These consumers, of their own volition, have taken every possible step to conserve their dwindling supply. There are also the heedless and careless who will not see, and this government would be failing in its duty if it neglected to take such steps by order as are necessary to protect both the welfare of our citizens and the operation of our industries.
I must advise the house that a new directive will be issued requiring suppliers of coal in the central provinces to maintain sufficient stock to protect the requirements of those conI Mr. Howe.]
sumers such as hospitals, public utilities, food processing plants, et cetera, whose continuing operation is essential to the health and safety of the country.
This order also sets up a scheme of priorities on the delivery of any coal, over and above that necessary to protect the previously mentioned essential requirements. Other orders will probably be necessary in the near future, and I shall endeavour to keep the house fully informed on any prospective action.
Every possible step is being taken to use our Canadian coal resources to the practical limit, to maintain industry in operation. At the present time, practically all the available surplus of bituminous coal in both eastern and western Canada is being directed to the central provinces, and consideration is being given to the possibility of supplying some quantities of the sub-bituminous and other fuels.
I would appeal to both the miners and the management in our Canadian coal industry to put forth their utmost effort to increase production, and provide some measure of relief and protection to their fellow citizens.
I would say, Mr. Speaker, that unless the production and transportation of coal is resumed in the United States in the near future, the central provinces of Canada are threatened with nothing less than a calamity, and that our people and our industry may be faced with hardship and distress on a scale never experienced during the war years.
These remarks refer to the supply of bituminous or soft coal for use by industry and other large consumers, and I now turn to the supply of other coals for domestic heating.
Anthracite has been entering the country in about the same volume as last year but, even if supply is maintained at this level, there will not be enough anthracite to supply the requirements. Negotiations on the renewal of the present labour contract are under way in the United States between the miners' union and the operators. This contract expires on May 31, and notice has been served by the union that work will cease at that date if a satisfactory contract is not signed. Regardless of possible strike action our supplies of anthracite have, of course, been stopped by the railway strike, and even if this strike is settled in the near future, the dislocation in normal rail traffic will prevent full supply for some time. A definite possibility of a stoppage of production is a threat of extending into future weeks or months.
Some action had already been taken to maintain the supply of suitable fuel for domestic purposes by retaining the government coke

Coal-Supply Situation
plant at Hamilton in operation. Since this and other coke plants in Ontario and Quebec use United States bituminous coal to a major extent, it will not be possible to count upon full production until bituminous coal is again available. Canadian coal is being directed to some coke plants to maintain operations on a reduced scale and prevent damage to the ovens, and this movement will be increased to the limit of the supply available.
I would advise the house that this phase of the coal problem dealing with the supply of domestic coal, which directly affects the health and welfare of every citizen, is a matter of the deepest concern. It may well be that, even with the most drastic action on the part of government, the individual consumer will have to reduce his fuel consumption in the coming winter. As soon as the situation in the United States is clarified I propose to advise the house in detail of the action taken and proposed by government to meet the serious emergency that we will have to face.

speechtext: The purpose of my question is to give information to the ordinary laymen of Canada who do not know much about the technical aspects of the coal problem. maintopic: STRIKE OF BARTENDERS IN ALBERTA
speechtext:
The capacity of the mines in Canada to produce, even at low points of consumption by industry, has never been stepped up to such an extent that Canadian production could take care of anything like the full requirements of this country. As my hon. friend knows, the coal of Canada is on the east coast, in Nova Scotia, and in the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia. Arrangements have been in effect for many years subsidizing freight rates into the central areas, so that it has been possible to ship Nova Scotia and

Nova Scotia and Alberta coal has been placed on a competitive basis with United States coal, but still our production in Canada is now something less than forty per cent of our total requirements, and only last winter quantities of American coal were shipped as far east as Truro, Nova Scotia. The western mines have supplied the needs of the prairies, apd have shipped a certain amount of coal to central Canada, but even under the conditions of full production that have obtained for the last several years the additional supplies from the prairies have filled the needs of only a small part of the market in the central provinces.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, May 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie that the house go into committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Bracken, and the amendment to the amendment of Mrs. Strum.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
When the house rose last evening, Mr. Speaker, we were discussing two amendments to the motion to go into supply. I was dealing with what I regard as the growing inequity to farmers arising from the government's administration of its price and wage policies. I had explained to the house that the amendment deals with two points: first, the depressing effect of the government's recent administration of its price and wage control policies on the production of food; and second, what I regard as the growing inequity being forced upon farmers by allowing increases in their costs of production without corresponding increases in the prices of their products.
With respect to the first matter, namely the effect on the production of food, I had endeavoured to show three things: first, that agricultural production, which increased year by year during the war, up to 1944, since that time had been decreasing; second, that agricultural production was decreasing more rapidly at the present time than during similar months in either of the last two years; third, that while that decrease was partly due to the weather, over which we have no control, it was also partly due to the policies of the government, over which it has full control.
With respect to the second question, namely that of the growing inequity to the rural population, I was about to attempt to show three things: First, that farm costs were being allowed to rise; second, that farm prices were not being allowed to rise accordingly, and, third-and the result of the other two-there is a growing inequity, to the disadvantage of the rural population. I think that is a fair statement of the argument respecting this part of. the main amendment.
What is the evidence with respect to increases in farm costs and no compensating increases in farm prices? I propose to recite three or four sets of facts. Let me turn first to the increases which have been allowed in price ceilings on non-farm products. Many of these were outlined by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) and by some other hon. members; therefore I shall not review them in detail. But to state a few: A 124 per cent increase in the ceiling price of farm machinery; a 16 to 20 per cent increase in certain types of bedding and upholstered furniture; 4 cents per quart increase in the price of Barbados molasses; increases ranging from less than 5 per cent to 10 per cent in finished paper and paper products; a suspension in the ceilings on a number of less essential converted paper products; increases approximating 85 per ton on steel ingots, and the resulting

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
increases in large numbers of products of which steel is the raw material; an 8 per cent increase in the wholesale price of lumber; an increase in the ceiling on gasoline in western Canada of two cents per gallon.
I place these on record only to illustrate whaT is being done that increases the cost of production to the farmers. In addition to that, the government's policy to subsidize production is now being changed. The wartime prices and trade board have indicated that in
1945	they paid $107 million in subsidies; in
1946	they expect it will be about $99 million, and the estimate for the next year is that it will be between $60 and $75 million, or a reduction of from $30 million to $40 million in those subsidies.
Another set of facts which illustrates to farmers these costs is found in the increase in wholesale prices. That index has been rising every month since September of last year; and, what is more, the rate of increase is becoming greater.
Since September the annual rate of increase each month has been as follows: October, November and December of last year, at a rate of 2-3 per cent per year; January, 8-3 per cent; February 7-1 per cent. Then, while in March there is a drop to 3-5 per cent, in April there- is an estimated increase to approximately 11 per cent. In other words for the past three months the rate of increase in wholesale prices is close to the average rate of increase from January to October 1941, before the price ceiling policy was instituted. When we consider the numerous examples of black market activities and the loss in quality of goods, the present rate of increase in wholesal price levels is probably nearly as much as it was just before the price ceiling policy began. In other words, we no longer have a stabilized price ceiling policy, because the government itself has broken it.
Another set of facts has to do with the increases in farm costs. Here again we take our statistics from government departments. Prices of agricultural products were unfair at the beginning of the war, to the extent of 20 per cent. When this policy was established it attempted to freeze the prices of farm products at a point 20 per cent below parity. Through constant pressure on the government some price ceilings have been raised from time to time, but generally speaking those changes came too late.
We need not go into the many changes which were made from them until 1943. Perhaps it is sufficient to say that by 1943 a reasonably acceptable relationship between the prices of farm products and the cost of
equipment required on the farms had been achieved. The point I make Is that, with the exception of two or three recent and minor changes, the majority of these farm products ceilings and subsidies have been constant for two or three years. They have been relatively constant, with the exception of these minor changes, but at the same time farm costs have been going up.
To what extent have those costs been going up? The index of the cost of things farmers buy stood in 1943 at 102-8, while today it is estimated to be 110-8, or an increase of approximately 8 per cent.
I might mention here that farm labour costs have more than doubled what they were in 1939, and they are 40 per cent more than in 1943, when this relationship for agriculture was established. If that relationship was approximately .fair in 1943, then it is definitely out of line to-day because costs have risen to a greater extent than have ^prices.
That is the point I wish to make, namely that this policy has discouraged production and that it is creating an inequity that this house ought not to allow, an inequity which affects a great section of the rural population. Another evidence of this fact is to be found in the small increases introduced by the government since this motion appeared on the order paper. It will be sufficient to men- ' tion only a few of them: The removal of the two per cent consumer subsidy on milk; the proposed removal in September of the producer subsidy of 55 cents per 100 pounds; the temporary increase from 35 cents to 55 cents per hundred until September; the in- . crease of four cents a pound on butter; an increase on hogs; an increase of 10 cents a hundred just the other day on milk entering into the production of cheese; and an increase of 8 cents a hundred on milk used in the production of concentrated milk products Those are the minor increases that have been given to this great industry, while costs all along the line have been going up. That, together with the fear in the farmers' minds that later on prices are not going to be so good, is the reason for the abandonment of farms in this and' other parts of Ontario. It is causing the farmer to say, "If we cannot make a little more out of this than we put into it, we will slow up until conditions get better." With farm labour difficult to get, with farm labour higher in price, with only about one out of five of the boys who left the farms during the war to go into munition work at high pay coming back, with farmers growing older and finding these difficult labour conditions to face, not having the same patriotic impulse to produce that they had during the
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

war, many are not now feeling the necessity of putting their shoulders into it as they did. and the result is decreased production.
What the farmers are afraid of to-day is the return of conditions similar to what they have had to face in the past. What were those conditions? Let me take one product as an example, because it is easy to state-the history of the price of wheat. In the depth' of the depression they received forty cents per bushel, the lowest figure in four hundred years. A few years later they received sixty cents per bushel. When some of us tried to get that raised to eighty cents we succeeded only to the extent of having it raised to seventy cents. The initial price went up to only ninety cents per bushel during the first two or three years of the war, and then in 1943 it was raised to $1.25. There was something from participation certificates to go on top of that.
I contend that we should try to retain at least as good as the recent relationship because it was considered to be relatively fair on the basis of what some people have chosen to call parity, which in some respects is not a fair or wholly acceptable relationship. Farmers are afraid of even that relationship being departed from, and so am I. That is why this amendment has been moved. In this connection I should like to read what was said by a gentleman who is now president of the organization which is trying to relieve famine in much of the world. The Minister of Agriculture met him in New York. I am not suggesting that we should have the same prices or the same wages that they have in the United States. We can have satisfactory conditions here if we have a right relationship between farm prices and wages. I quote from the Ottawa Citizen of May 22, 1946, as follows:
Criticism of low prices paid to Canadian farmers for their products was expressed by UNRRA Director F. H. LaGuardia at the united nations food and agriculture conference yesterday.
He said nations cannot get away with "squeezing their farmers" any more. Farmers must be able to earn decent incomes if nations are to prosper because farmers are industry's best customers.
President Roosevelt understood this, and obtained legislation ensuring parity between agriculture and labour. This, however, has had a great bearing on Canada, resulting in disparities which must be adjusted.
Later Mr. LaGuardia explained to this bureau that the low prices of Canadian agricultural products are a constant threat to farmers in the United States, who fear they will be undersold in their own markets.
I have here also a report issued by the bureau of agricultural economics, United States Department of Agriculture, in which is

given the relative position of agriculture today in their economy. Taking the period prior to the last war as a basis of arriving at what they call the parity ratio, the index for 1945 is given as 116, with the present day figure being a little above that. That is what that nation has done for its agricultural industry. There has been some criticism over the fact that the agricultural organizations over there have been able to maintain a relatively better position for agriculture in their economy than what they regard as parity. I am not suggesting anything of the kind here. We want to get real parity, and we want to keep it and not let things drop back to where they were before.
Much has been said in this debate about the desirability of stabilized farm prices. The government has said it is trying to stabilize the situation and not let it get out of control. Speaker after speaker has said that we want stabilized farm prices. That all sounds very good, but it does not mean quite as much as it seems to. It is not only stabilized prices the farmer wants; it is a stabilized net income. If we stabilize farm prices and let farm costs go up, that will be the best way I know of to bring about the bankruptcy of our farmers.
It is somewhat comparable to the position of the wage earner. What he needs is not so much a higher hourly rate of pay, but a higher annual income. What he needs is not so much a stabilized hourly wage as a wage related to the cost of living. What agriculture needs is not only stabilized prices but prices that bear a right relationship to costs, particularly when they are increasing.
What are the facts with respect to this matter? The government has allowed its wage control policy to be broken time after time. I am not saying this by way of criticism at the moment, but it has happened. It has allowed the price ceilings to be broken in ways that have been outlined here by different speakers. In defence it has pointed to the danger of inflation, which is a real danger. But even while it points to the danger of inflation it continues to practice policies which increase that danger. Nor am I at the moment criticizing those policies; I am simply pointing to the fact that they do increase the danger. What are some of these government policies?
Samples of these inflationary policies are deficit financing to the extent of $2,500 million a year; large foreign loans; reduction in consumer subsidies; the elimination of certain import subsidies, and high, or if I may be allowed to say so, in some cases extravagant, government expenditures. All this has created

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
a backlog of purchasing power which is bound to break out somewhere and is breaking out in the form of the black markets that we have to-day. There is a growing lack of respect for law, which in turn has created the need of an army of agents to try to enforce the law. All these are difficulties with which the government has to deal. What is the answer? What are some of the evidences of this backlog of purchasing power?
Let me mention a few. The average monthly deposits in banks in 1939 were $2,600 million; now they are $5,700 million. The increase in savings accounts of $5,000 or less from 1940 to 1944 has been over $600 million. Bank deposits and currency in 1939 were S224 per capita; they are now $458. Notes in the hands of the public in February, 1946, were five times as great as in the pre-war period. The total of war bonds purchased amounts to over $12,000 million. This represents withdrawals as future purchasing power equal to one and one-third times the entire national income for last year. It is this backlog of purchasing power which is sure to break out somewhere and which is the cause of the black market we have now-the worst black market, in my judgment, this nation has ever had.
AVhat is the antidote? The government tries to hold the line. One antidote is to increase production of the products in short supply, the products *which the people want, and, particularly in time of war, the production of food. The best way to encourage the production of food is to give some incentive to provide more food rather than to withdraw some of the incentives we have had. We must give the farmers a square deal: that is the whole contention of this amendment.
With respect to the subamendment, it is a legitimate subject of discussion, but, I suggest, not at th.e expense of discarding altogether the amendment with respect to the effect of the government's policy on food production. With parts of the subamendment I agree. It is unjustifiable to increase farmers' costs without increasing their prices. Whether it is justifiable to increase the prices of steel and farm machinery on some other grounds is a question which I expect the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Ilsley) to deal with. It has already been discussed by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Mayhew), perhaps by others. To the extent the government can show that the cost of labour or of materials entering into the production of these things makes these increases necessary, all those who believe in giving enterprise a fair deal will have to support the government's position. The government has made a pretty good defence. It has outlined how much thp 'ost of labour
entering into the production of steel and farm machinery has increased. I do not remember exactly the figures, but I believe it was indicated that the increase is much more than * the increase which has been granted these industries. So far as those who are associated with me are concerned, if the government can justify those increases on the grounds I have mentioned we shall have no alternative but to support the government in this particular respect, because we cannot stand for a fair deal for the farmers alone and for labour alone, and deny fair treatment to those who invest their money in industries which produce needed goods and provide needed employment. If the government is too generous to these concerns, we shall vote against them; so long as they are only fair to industry, we shall support them, and I look forward to hearing what the Acting Prime Minister has to say on the matter.
As regards my own amendment, I believe the meaning is .plain even though the wording may not be quite so clear as some think it should be. If the government's policy is discouraging the production of food in a time of famine, or even if it is failing to encourage the production of more food in times like these, the amendment deserves support. If the government's recent administration of the price ceiling and other control policies- and I am criticizing recent administration, not so much the administration prior to the last six months-is putting farmers in a less favourable position, the amendment should be supported; and to the extent that it is supported it will be a guide and in some degree an instruction to the government to increase farm prices at least to the same extent that it increases farm costs.

But, if the farmer receives an increase in the price of farm products, that increase will raise the cost of living to industrial workers, and the lower the wage or salary the greater the increase will be. That is so because the worker spends a greater proportion of his wage or salary on food than the highest paid workers. The person receiving $700 a year, and having a wife and family to support, spends a greater proportion of the $700 on food than the person receiving $1,500 or $2,500 does. Therefore immediately you increase the cost of food you lower the standard of living of the low-income industrial workers. It is for that reason we say

and I have insisted on this all along-that the stabilization of prices has always been carried on the backs, or on the stomachs, of the low-paid workers of Canada.

The depression has, furthermore, demonstrated that the strong and the organized are attaining an ever-increasing position of dominance in our economic life; that economic power is becoming concentrated. With this concentration, old theories of economic control are proving inadequate.

But I also told them if it was a straight vote of want of confidence I would vote with the government-and on this occasion I intend to do that.
I am even more convinced that I should vote with the government, after listening to hon. members opposite. What would happen in Canada if the leader of the opposition were to lift all price ceilings? What would happen to the people if this government were put out and the party led by the leader of the opposition were to take its place?

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: There would be great progress in Canada.

speechtext:
I do not know what name the Progressive Conservative party would use, if it were in power, or under what leader it would be.
I speak briefly this afternoon, one of my reasons being that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) refused to take my advice. I speak to him-in a most kindly way, of course. When I spoke to him before he made a flippant answer on a matter of vital importance not only to British Columbia, but to all the people of Canada, and after listening to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) we realize that it is a matter of importance to the people of the whole world. What we need most .in the world to-day is foodstuffs. In British Columbia, in my district and the district of the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), we are being faced with the necessity of dumping fruits because we are not able to obtain the crates, hallocks and barrels needed for the fruit now being grown. The reasons are different from those given by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). Apparently my services are in demand, because I got the following note,-not from the Minister of Labour:
The Minister of Labour will see you now, and immediately you have settled the timber strike President Truman will see you in the White House.
I do not know who sent me that note. I enjoyed my last trip to Washington and I should be glad to go down again. I suggest to my hon. friend that we have plenty of troubles of our own to settle; let the United States look after theirs. I am not going to go into the timber situation to-day, in deference
to my friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley), who is acting as leader of the government. I understand he wants to have this debate brought to a close and a vote taken before six o'clock; therefore I shall be brief. But I intend to have something to say about the timber situation on Monday. I have a solution to offer to the Minister of Labour with which I think the hon. member for Vancouver East will agree.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Why wait until Monday?

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I did not want to take up too much time to-day, but I think I will take a full forty-two minutes on Monday. To-day I want to justify my stand in connection with ceilings. To the best of my knowledge I am the only member who insisted on the ceiling being taken off the prices of strawberries and raspberries. That may seem strange action on the part of a member who disapproves the removal of ceilings from all farm products, but small fruits are in an entirely different category, since they are perishable. I approached the wartime prices and trade board and asked that the announcement of the removal of this ceiling be made by April 1 in order that the producers in the Fraser valley could order the necessary crates, hallocks and barrels for S02 berries and other fruits. Replying to a question asked by an hon. member on the other side, the Minister of Finance said that we could not expect an industrial firm to produce at a loss. I do not know how the wartime prices and trade board can justify the stand they took in expecting the farmer to produce at a loss. Before these farmers could order the necessary crates, hallocks and barrels, they had to know whether the ceiling would be taken off, but that announcement was not made until much later. I am not going to weary the house with the dates, but that was released on the same day that I was given permission to release the information. The result is that these producers have not the necessary crates, hallocks and barrels for S02 berries and other fruits. Some soArtion must be arrived at, and on Monday I hope to suggest a solution to the Minister of Labour so far as British Columbia is concerned.
Unless a solution is arrived at it will be necessary to dump these fruits instead of their being preserved to be sent to the people of starving Europe. I blame this situation on the officials of the wartime prices and trade board. As I said before, there is no practical agricultural man on that board. I was not given permission to release this information earlier because they said it .would work to the detriment of the producers in being able to make
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

a deal with the manufacturers of these supplies. I replied, "Who knows best, the producers' association or some clerk?" I will not use language such as that used by an hon. gentleman the other night, but the fact is that some of these clerks down at the wartime prices and trade board have not and never had any knowledge of small fruits. As I have said before, the sooner we put agriculture back into the hands of the Department of Agriculture, the better it will be for the producer and the consumer.
I should like to refer briefly to milk. I think the dairy producers in British Columbia will agree with me when I say that I think the government made a mistake in establishing a consumer subsidy of two cents a quart. At that time the people were prosperous; our workers were getting high wages, but now we have unemployment, our veterans are coming home from overseas, and this subsidy is to be taken off. I do not agree with the leader of the opposition that all ceiling prices should be taken off, because if that were done, things would be worse for the farmer. If a policy of subsidy payments is put into effect, then that policy should be continued while ceilings are on, and at a proper level.
I do not think the federation of agriculture will agree that the increase from twenty to thirty cents on cheese is sufficient, and the same observation would apply to the increase on milk from fifteen to twenty-three cents. I understand that a final decision has not been reached on this matter, that it is still open, and I would urge that the producers' representatives be called in and consulted. I do not want to take up any more time because as I tell my friend the Minister of Labour, I intend to take up forty-two minutes if I am permitted on Monday to explain exactly how the lumber strike in British Columbia can be settled.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Cruickshank) has warned/ us about what he is going to do on Monday so that w7e do not necessarily have to be here. I am glad to have this opportunity of saying a few words on this matter. I understand it is hoped that ,the debate will be concluded before the house rises at six.
I shall endeavour to complete in a very few minutes what I want to say.
In the first place I am opposed to the removal of price ceilings at this time because I believe in price control1. I believe that unquestionably the object of the amendment under discussion is to remove those controls. The action taken by the government has given
[.Mr. Cruickshank.]
some excuse to the opposition to come to parliament and) demand that changes be made. Increases have been permitted in commodities such as steel, oil and farm implements.
The Conservative party, with "Progressive" tacked on, has moved this amendment:
This house is of the opinion that the government's price ceiling policies with respect to farm products are discouraging production of needed food and imposing on the food producers of Canada an unfair share of the burden of maintaining the government's price stabilization policies.
To me that means only one thing-the intention to remove all price controls from agricultural products. If that was not what the opposition meant, then they should have said this:
This house is of the opinion that the government's price ceiling policies with respect to farm machinery are discouraging production of needed food and imposing on the food producers of Canada an unfair share of the burden of maintaining the government's price stabilization policies.
That would have made it quite clear that what the opposition wanted to do was to increase farm prices to equal the increase in the production cost occasioned by the increase in the prices of farm implements.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: That was the intention of the amendment.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
If that was the intention of the amendment, then I think it was ambiguously worded. I do not question the word of my hon. friend, and I have no doubt that was his intention, but it is unfortunate he failed to convey his intention to those whom he is leading.
In the course of his speech the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) was asked this direct question by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley):	"Is it not the
announced policy of the Progressive party to remove the ceiling from prices of farm products?"

party."

Well, "progressively" Conservative party. Perhaps I had better quote Hansard, page 1785:
Mr. Ilsley: Is it not the announced policy of the Progressive Conservative party to remove the ceiling from prices of farm products?
That was the question of the Minister of Finance. The reply of the hon. member for Lake Centre was this:
Mr. Diefenbaker: There is no argument about that.

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
That is settled so far as our party is concerned; that is beyond all cavil. "I am . speaking", says he, "about the entire ceiling." We do not want to remove the entire ceiling, we just want to remove the ceiling on the price of farm products. That in effect is the statement of one of the most effective debaters and supporters of the bon. gentleman who moved this amendment. So I think it is unfortunate that, while his intention was, as he says, to achieve something far different from that which is stated in the amendment, his party following was not informed of the fact.
The government started all this fuss by permitting the increase of prices on steel and, particularly, on farm implements. The government has told us that careful investigation was made and that it was discovered that sufficient profits could not be made by those industries unless this increase was given. I pointed out when we were discussing that particular increase, and others have said pretty much the same thing, that an increase of price of one commodity would go right down through the whole economy of the state. Already that is beginning to be felt. Farmers, wage earners and people on fixed incomes will be particularly affected by the alteration of any important commodity price. Although I believe in price control, while I am not saying there should be no alteration in it at any time for the purpose of maintaining the balance-everybody understands that that is implied in price control-I suggest that before the government granted an increase of prices to the industries I have mentioned they should have caused a survey to be taken of the wage earners' incomes and standards of living as compared with, say, the standards of living of those who are running the implement manufacturing business and the manufacturers of steel.
I am not going to quote figures at this time, but those who have studied this question will admit that the average income of the wage earners and the farmers of this country is far below that which has been found to be necessary to provide a reasonably decent standard of living. If anyone disputes that statement I would refer him to Doctor Marsh's report, which was published not very long ago, and I think it will be also agreed that since the publication of his report standards of living have not risen but have rather been lowered;, because prices have risen where wages have "not been correspondingly increased. Even without the increase which was granted to manufacturers of agricultural implements these people would stand a far better chance of making a very good profit than the average
working man and the average farmer of Canada stands to make a fair living. Now that the increase has been granted of "bourse the fat is in the fire; we shall have to go on increasing prices and wages until we meet ourselves coming back like the hon. member who has recently left the chamber, who spoke yesterday and who goes round in circles so much.
I would not like to be a party to the removal of price control. The amendment moved by the leader of the opposition means only one thing, the removal of price control. I want, if possible, to use my vote in such a way as to increase farm prices and wages to equal the increases already made in other commodities which enter into their costs of living and of production, but I want at the same time to support adequate price control. What the government should have done, rather than increase prices, was to take over the manufacture of farm implements, or alternatively to make it possible for the agricultural industry to get control of this manufacturing industry on a cooperative basis and produce its own implements at cost. I do not believe that the industry as it now stands is producing sufficient implements to meet the needs of agriculture. When these things happened during the war the government knew what to do and stepped in and did it. It produced the goods and won the war. Now it is charged with winning the peace. We need goods now in peace time just as badly as we did during the war, and the government is hoping by raising these prices a little to do the job, without recognizing that its action imposes a tremendous burden on the great masses of the people. I suggest then that instead of having done this they should have taken over the industry and operated it as a government institution, and then if there was a loss it would be borne by all the people of Canada rather than be placed upon the backs of agriculture. Better still, I think, it should have taken the advice of the agriculture committee in its report as contained in the journals of the house for 1937:
34. That the companies themselves-
Speaking of the implement companies.
-should make every effort to reduce these costs or farmers should be encouraged to organize for the cooperative distribution and servicing of farm implements.
I hope that the government wall take notice of that suggestion and also remember that it is not merely my suggestion but the recommendation of a committee of this house, and will make it possible for the industry to be financed for the farmers and placed in their hands, in order that they may be per-
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

mitted to have control, to some extent at least, of some of the costs which enter into their production. If the controls were all removed from farm prices, as has been suggested specifically by hon. members speaking for the Progressive Conservative party, it would commit agriculture to the mercy of open market operations. We have a long experience of that, and the farmers have not been satisfied with it.
Every member in this house knows that when the farmer was on the free private enterprise basis he had no chance because he happened to be. the one man in the country who was not able to make his own prices, to add costs and profit to the price of his commodities, and the only organization that can make prices for the farmer is the government. The government for the past few years has been making prices for the farmer, and during that period the farmers have been better off than perhaps they have ever been in their history. That is now being forgotten. The government itself is weakening somewhat on the question of the control of prices.
In the old days the Conservatives and Liberals did the same thing, though they professed to believe differently. We all know what happened in the old days of the tariff debates. The Conservatives wanted to raise the tariff and the Liberals did not want it raised, but the Liberals usually did the raising and the Conservatives lowered it. Now the Conservatives openly wish to remove price ceilings, while the Liberals say they want to have the ceilings still there, and yet they proceed to remove them. That is the position as I see it.
It may be popular to advocate the removal of farm price ceilings at the moment. While there is no doubt that if the controls were removed, the price of wheat and prices of [DOT]other farm products would rise rapidly for a time, in the long-range view that would be a disastrous policy to follow. Incidentally, it is being adopted by the government itself jnwittingly. But just as surely as other commodity prices have been raised, so surely will the farmers demand an increase and there will be no excuse for not giving it to them. It will have to be given; the same will be true of labour, .and those of us who try to hold on to price controls will have to throw in our lot with the underdog in demanding a corresponding rise in his income.
I wish to maintain price controls. I want wages and farm incomes increased so that the standard of living of those people will be equal to that of the manufacturers who received 12J per cent increase. government maintaining controls; but they would be very much afraid if the C.C.F. got into power, because they know that we would stand for planned economy, and so they centred their attack on us. Then they say that they are the party of the farmers. That is really an amusing statement, coming as it does from the Conservative party. I am afraid that it needs more than the Progressive appendage to guarantee that. One of the ve#y principles of conservatism is that there are certain things that always remain the same-particularly the Conservative party. That being so, it has a long history which accounts for what it is now. It can never be other than what it is. It cannot cut itself away from its past. It is very much like this; I am not saying it with any implications at all to any hon. member or to anybody in this house. You can call a donkey "Bessie", but it would not shorten its ears or weaken its kick or make it a little bit more human than it was before. You can call the Conservative party "progressive", but the Conservative party can never get away from its past. speechtext:
We have had a long debate on the amendment of the leader of the opposition, which reads as follows:
This house is of the opinion that the government's price ceiling policies with respect to farm products are discouraging production of needed food and imposing on the food producers of Canada an unfair share of the burden of maintaining the government's price stabilization policies.
Also the amendment to the amendment, moved by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum):
This house is of the opinion that the government's policies of permitting recent unjustifiable

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
increases in the prices of farm machinery and of steel have resulted in imposing on food producers and workers of Canada an unfair share of the burden of maintaining the government's price stabilization policies.
There has been much attack and crossattack between the members of the Progressive Conservative party and the members of the C.C.F., and naturally there has been much attack upon the government by the members of both parties. This afternoon I should like to speak rather seriously, and without attempting to reply to attacks, of a political character at least, that have been made upon the government, but in defence of the government's price stabilization policy. Most of the speeches in this debate have been against the government, though there have been some excellent speeches from this side of the house in defence of the policies we are following.
We instituted the price ceiling policy in the fall of 1941, and continued that policy with great rigidity until recently in respect of everything except farm prices and wages, and perhaps fish and products of that kind. The figures I used in speaking to the house in a previous debate on farm implement prices indicate that the treatment which was accorded between 1941 and 1946 to what is called industry was entirely different from the treatment accorded to the primary producers and the wage-earners of this country. The number of wage increases that have been allowed; the extent of the wage increase that have been allowed; the number of price rises and subsidy payments which have been used to increase the returns to primary producers, have been very extensive and very great. I put some of those figures on record when I spoke to the house on that other occasion. The net result of the figures is that the level of farm prices in Canada, including subsidies, has risen 44 per cent since the basic period in the fall of 1941, not including the wheat participation certificates which would add several more units per cent. But with regard to the great range of commodities in this country, the price ceiling has been rigidly maintained. I believe that was the right policy to follow. It was a policy followed in the face of great pressure and much opposition; nevertheless it was a policy which by ingenuity and firmness we were able to follow during those years without putting people out of business.
When I say there was rigidity, there was not complete rigidity. There were price increases, some of them on unimportant products and some on more important products, during the years. But we finally came to the time when more flexibility had to be introduced. Conditions changed to such an extent, with the disappearance of war business and when the cumulative effect of wage and price increases, which entered into costs, began to be felt, that it was entirely unreasonable to expect certain industrial producers to carry on, because they would be obliged to carry on at a loss. I understand that the attitude of the Progressive Conservative party-and I am not speaking technically now; I am not speaking to the language of the amendment-has been made abundantly clear in this debate, as well as outside this house; and I believe that the policy of the Progressive Conservative party is the complete removal of ceilings on the prices of farm products. Am I correct?

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: May I comment there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: I may say to the Acting Prime Minister that, while that is the objective of the party, it is not a part of this resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
That is exactly what I said. That is the objective of the party and the policy of the party:	the immediate removal
of all ceilings on farm products. Of course, if that policy were put into effect all ceilings would go almost immediately.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: With all respect, the minister is not speaking of this resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Well, I do not think we can take a legalistic view of the resolution, though I think the leader of the opposition did.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Just take a realistic view of what the amendment actually says.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
The policy is clear, and it has been reiterated in this debate. Apart altogether from the resolution, I wish to point out to the house and to the people of Canada the disastrous consequences of implementing a policy calling for the complete removal of the ceiling on prices of farm products. Then the cost of living at once takes a great rise, with this condition of world shortage and national shortage in so many foods. When that rise in the cost of living takes place the effect on wages is immediate and violent. The effect on prices of manufactured goods is immediate and violent, leading at once to further increases in wages and further increases in prices of farm products. So that the policy of this government is not the removal of the ceilings on all farm products. It is the control of prices of farm products, which we will try to operate as fairly as possible in a period of very great difficulty.
If it had been possible for us to refrain from making any changes whatever in wages, in prices of industrial products and in prices of
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

farm products, despite the rigidity of that position it would have been perhaps the easiest to take. But, as I say, you come to a place in this operation when war industry disappears; when the effects of all these increases in prices through the years begin to take sharp effect; when you have to make adjustments upward, and then we enter into the most difficult phase of price control operations. As I understand the position of the C.C.F., in theory it is not very much different from the position of the government in regard to price control, with one or two qualifications.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Improvements.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: I cannot agree that they are improvements. In the early part of the debate, when I listened to the leader of the C.CE., I thought that he was in favour of continuing rigidity; that if you back up here, you must back up somewhere else, so that we,should not back up at all. I thought that was the position. But, of course, after some prodding from members of the Progressive Conservative party, the C.C.F. speakers were driven to the point of saying that they would like to see some prices go up, that there had to be an orderly upward ' adjustment of prices, and so on, but that it must be done on what was called a scientific basis.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: I said that on March 27. I have my speech before me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Then I am wrong in my interpretation of the attitude which I thought was the initial attitude of C.C.F. speakers in the debate. It will be understood that I am not trying to make political gain against them; I am just trying to clarify the situation. In theory, their position is not very different from that of the government with regard to this matter. They say that there must be other adjustments, and that the process, while a very difficult one to operate equitably, is a process which must go on.
But if I understand the speeches which C.C.F. members have made I do think this- and it is not a point which has been made very clear in the debate-that they believe in permanent price control. That is, they believe that it is not something which we should go out of, but rather that it is something incidental to a planned economy, that if we do not have permanent price control certain parts of the community will suffer and that therefore we should institute a permanent policy of price control.
That is constitutionally impossible, whether it is economically possible, or not. Having had some experience with provincial premiers, I know perfectly well it would be impossible

to get an amendment to the constitution which would permit our embarking upon a policy of indefinite price control. Holding the views I do, I do not think it would be economically justifiable. I know, from the experience I have had as the minister under whom the wartime prices and trade board operates, it is just agony of the most acute kind, where we go from a period of war; during which a great many people say to the government, "Whatever you say we will do, because we are at war", to a period when each man is aggressively asserting his own individuality. I know it is just about impossible for any central authority to exercise any logical and consistent price control over a long period of time.
Therefore the government has announced a policy of progressive decontrol, and in recent months some of the ceilings have been taken off entirely. Usually in a case where an apparent balance has been struck between demand and supply, or a position has been arrived at which appears to be reasonably permanent, the government, in such instances, has taken ceilings off entirely. In other cases the ceilings have been adjusted.
The amendments of both the C.C.F. and the Progressive Conservative party condemn the government for having been unfair to agriculture, either in its policy or in its administration of policies. I cannot admit that that has been so. I can say to the house that certainly we tried not to be unfair to agriculture. One can understand that when the government is putting ceilings on this, that and the other thing, endless arguments can be developed as to whether one is fair or not. People in this world have a habit of seeing things their own way, and opinions differ as to what is fair to oneself. But, by the ordinary tests that can be applied, I suggest that the administration of our stabilization policy has been fair to agriculture.
For one thing, one might take the difference between the relationship of prices of farm products in 1945 and prices of fully and chiefly manufactured goods. I have before me a chart which I believe would be of interest to the house. That chart shows that the relationship of prices of farm products to prices of manufactured goods in 1945 was more favourable to the farmer than in any other year in the past fifty-six years, with the exception of one year, 1917, during the first world war. That is to say, the price level of farm products is farther above the price level of fully and chiefly manufactured goods than it has ever been since 1890 with, as I say, the exception of the year 1917. If we take the test of parity, again I would say that everyone

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
has a different definition. However, let us take the period 1926-29 as the basis of parity, a period which apparently is regarded as being a favourable one for the
farmers, and which is usually referred to as the basis of parity. Official figures from the bureau of statistics show that in March, 1946, the average wholesale prices of Canadian farm products was six per cent higher than the average of 1926-29, and that is without making any allowance for wheat participation payments. I am informed that if wheat participation payments were added, instead of being six per cent the figure would be something like ten per cent. Over the same period the official index of prices of commodities and services, including labour used by the farmers had, according to the bureau of statistics, increased by seven per cent. That is, the actual level of farm prices is slightly higher to-day than in 1926-29, and the relationship between prices of goods farmers sell, and prices of goods and services farmers buy is almost identical with that which prevailed in the former period of prosperity, the advantage being in favour of the farm prices. I have taken this period because it is the one frequently quoted in respect of parity.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) rather confirmed what I am saying on this point. He said-and very fairly, I thought -that up until six months ago, for the period up to and before that for some time, the relationship was reasonably satisfactory between farm prices and other prices.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Oh, well, only for the last three years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Yes, for the last three years, since 1943.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: And on this technical definition of parity, which I do not accept.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: At any rate, what the leader of the opposition said then, and what he says now confirms what I am saying. But he bases his arguments upon developments in the last few months. I have not had an opportunity of examining the figures which he gave with regard to the movement of wholesale or farm prices since that time, because those figures were used for the first time this afternoon. But the figures which he gave show that there had been an irregular movement of wholesale prices which, on balance, is upward. I suppose those were the wholesale prices of fully and chiefly manufactured goods and that is why there had been an irregular movement.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: It was regular except for one month.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: It went up; it went down; then it went up and it is higher than it was.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: It started at 2-3 and went to 11.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: I still submit that what I say is correct, that there has been an irregular upward movement during the last few months. The leader of the opposition also gave the increases in farm prices during the last few months. He gave quite a list of the adjustments that have been made and one would have to see how those compared-

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Would not it be just as well to let me finish? You have no idea how much I have listened to this week.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: I am listening to you and I would not have the Acting Prime Minister say that these recent increases amounted to very much.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
We shall never get anywhere if we are going to argue every little point. The leader of the opposition is basing his whole argument, not upon the price stabilization policy, not upon what has happened year after year and year after year, but upon what has happened in the last two or three months, since the first of the year. I have to take these figures and see whether they amount to anything. I have to balance the adjustment in farm prices against these others, and I have to see what is the trend and what are the prospects of there being further irregularities in these movements.
I am not putting forward these arguments with a view to saying that the price relationship is perfect or anything like that. I am not saying that total farm- cash income while very high by any standards is too high. All I am saying is that we are confronted, with an amendment, and I want hon. members, on this side of the house particularly, to understand that our price policy is being attacked vigorously by both oppositions in this house and that the administration of that price policy is being attacked vigorously by all oppositions in this house. It is being attacked on the ground that the administration has disregarded the farmer and has been unfair to agriculture.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: And to the worker.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
From the C.C.F., "the
worker". It is said that it has been unfair to the farmer and the worker, but the official opposition has contended mainly for the farmer. I am saying that when you apply some of these tests that are about the most valid tests that you can apply it will be seen

maintopic: BEVIBH EDITION

speechtext:
Price Ceiling-Farm Products
that the government through the wartime prices and trade board, and the government itself by its subsidy policy, has tried very hard and has succeeded reasonably well in maintaining a relationship which, on the whole, is favourable to agriculture.
Of course one of the main items of attack in this debate has been the attack on the price adjustment which was authorized for agricultural implements. There has been a large amount of discussion on that and it will be hard to answer some of the things that have been said. It will be impossible for me to answer them fully because a large number of speeches have been made and quite technical arguments have been advanced. I have already said a great deal of what I propose to say now about these adjustments.
To begin with, what was done by the wartime prices and trade board? One obvious thing should be pointed out, that the wartime prices and trade board did not order up these prices. All the wartime prices and trade board did was to say that if the companies put them up, they could not put them up more than 12% per cent at retail. It was not a case of putting up these prices; it was a case of saying that they could put them up only so much.

maintopic: BEVIBH EDITION
speechtext: That was plenty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BEVIBH EDITION
speechtext:
Just let me talk now. I am not very good at repartee and it throws me off if there are too many interruptions. I should like to go along without any interruption. When I spoke to this house before, I said that I had confidence in the price-fixing agency we have in this country. During the debate this week I have heard one speaker after another attack the wartime prices and trade board on one ground and another, and upon my word one would have thought that we had in Canada . a price control agency that was a bad one, that was something we should be ashamed of.
I am only saying what people everywhere are saying, and perhaps it is going a little too far for me to assert dogmaticallw that we have the best price control agency in the world. Compared with any price control agency that one hears about in any other country, the price control agency in the Dominion of Canada is recognized within this country and out of this country as being as conscientious, as competent, as resolute and as efficient as any body could be. I must shout that if necessary to the people and to this house because it is true that the price control agency we have in this country is a good price control agency.

maintopic: BEVIBH EDITION
speechtext: That cannot be refuted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BEVIBH EDITION
speechtext:
It is a little hard for me to take these attacks upon Mr. Gordon. It is within the privileges of hon. members to make them, but it is within my right to defend the wartime prices and trade board, and I hereby do so to the utmost of my ability. The wartime prices and trade board did not act speedily or hastily in this matter. They received applications from the implement companies as early as January for an increase in prices on the ground that with the loss of their war business, with the smaller volume that they would have thereby and with the increases in costs-some of them substantial- they were getting to a place in 1946 when it would be virtually impossible for them to do business if they were not permitted to advance their prices.
They advanced figures, but some of the critics have said that those were merely figures given by the companies and they would not be convinced anyway, that they ought to be investigated. Those figures were investigated as far as it was practical for an official agency to investigate figures. After a protracted investigation, the wartime prices and trade board came to the conclusion that ceilings should be lifted to this extent if we were to have production in this country this year. The production of agricultural implements in this country this year is very important.

maintopic: BEVIBH EDITION
speechtext: Did the wartime prices and trade board know of the stock bonus that was given to the officials?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BEVIBH EDITION
speechtext:
further increase in the price of farm implements although several had already been granted in the intervening period.
In consequence, it is clear that the companies will find it difficult to achieve the level of earnings which the board regarded as reasonable when it authorized the 124 per cent price adjustment on Canadian-made implements sold in Canada.
On the question of increases in costs, we have had a lot of interesting speeches. 'It was pointed out first by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle that when I said that wages in this industry had increased 284 Per cent, factory overhead had increased 23 per cent and the cost of materials had increased 20 per cent, I was not saying anything very important, because those percentages applied to only a small part of the retail price, and that the figure of percentage of direct labour employed in the manufacture of implements was given as very small. It is small in the farm implement industry. But direct labour is only part of the labour which enters into the cost of implements. The item of factory overhead, if I remember correctly, includes 70 per cent labour-what they call indirect labour-and while it is not a logical or a valid deduction to say that, because wages have gone up 284 per cent, or in the case of Massey-Harris, 33 per cent, according to the figures I gave the house before, they can reasonably expect the cost of their implements to go up that much;, while that must be conceded, nevertheless there is a substantial increase in over-all costs after allowing for the reduction in selling costs. The hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Argue) seemed to assume that there had been a 40 per cent reduction of selling costs since 1941. There has been only a 20 per cent reduction of selling costs since 1941; and 40 per cent reduction has been since the 1936-39 period, and if the hon- gentleman will look at the speech of the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.), he will see that that is the case.

maintopic: BEVIBH EDITION
speechtext: I would not wish to interrupt the minister, but I did not assume that it was from 1941 to 1945; I took the statement of the parliamentary assistant that it was a 40 per cent reduction from 1936.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BEVIBH EDITION
speechtext:
I thought on reading the hon. gentleman's speech that he did assume as I said, but if he did not, well and good.
I asked the wartime prices and trade board to go over the matter of increase in costs and arrive at' a figure of increased costs of production of these implements as a whole, not of any particular implement; and after going into the matter very carefully they have advised me that the actual net increase in

total costs as a percentage of the retail price has been approximately 15 per cent since 1941.
The hon. member for Wood Mountain got a considerably lower figure than that, but the figure arrived at by the wartime prices and trade board is an increase in total costs as a percentage of the retail price of approximately 15 per cent.
But that is only part of the story. Since then, the earnings of the companies have been adversely affected by the cancellation of war contracts. Indeed, because of the removal of war business, their total sales volume will be smaller in 1946 than in 1945. Some of the facilities used for war production are not suit-*able for the manufacture of implements and, in addition, shortages of materials are limiting the extent of expansion in implement output. The price adjustment which was authorized was based on all the relevant considerations, not on the position concerning one implement or group of implements or type of business. Costs were carefully examined. Estimated volume was studied. The proportion of export business was considered. All these factors and others entered into the decision. I cannot say that the increase on a given particular implement is the exact amount which theoretically might have beeij applied on that implement. The board simply could not have adjusted prices in that sort of detail. It had to look at the over-all position and to make the smallest practicable adjustment that was appropriate to the over-all position. That is precisely what the board did.
As I said at the beginning, we did not want to do this. We knew it was not exactly the sort of action that was calculated to add popularity to the government-increasing the price of farm implements. But one has to be fair about these matters. One has to be fair to industry as well as to agriculture. We cannot say that we are the party of any particular section of the community, as the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) said the other night. We have to look at the situation from the point of view of the people as a, whole, and we must therefore be fair to agriculture, to labour and also to business.
I am satisfied that this adjustment which was made was fair, that it was necessary, unless we were to treat the agricultural implement industry, just because it was the agricultural implement industry, on a basis different from that on which we treat all other industries.
I do not think I have very much more to say. As I said at the opening of my remarks, I have no apologies whatever to make for the wartime prices and trade board, and the work that it has done for this country since it

Price Ceiling-Farm, Products
was set up at the beginning of the war. I repeat, I have no apologies to offer for it to-day.	. .	, . ,
We cannot take the position, which the Progressive Conservative party is taking, that we must remove at once all ceilings from prices of agricultural products, because in a very few weeks that" would bring ruin to the whole population of Canada. That is an irresponsible position to take.

maintopic: BEVIBH EDITION
speechtext: That is not what the resolution says.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BEVIBH EDITION
speechtext: Their resolution does not say that, but everyone else says it. If I understand the position of the C.C.F. party, I cannot share their view that we should not decontrol, that we should go on permanently as we are. Wb cannot do that constitutionally, nor do I think it would be practical from an economic point of view. I do not for one moment admit their position; I assert the very contrary. I assert that in this particular instance of agricultural implements we have acted with great care, with fairness and with moderation and have authorized an increase which was no more than was necessary to make it possible and probable that we should get the maximum production of agricultural implements in 1946.	-
